P267.identity_reference: Solar-operated interlayer electrothermal evaporator enabling instant high-flux freshwater production across multiple scenarios; DOI 10.1038/s44221-026-00734-6
P267.user_provided_abstract: As conflicts and frequent natural disasters intensify, timely access to freshwater from multiple resources is extremely important for human survival. Electrothermal desalination is a promising solution for the development of green energy-driven, miniaturized and high-flux systems. However, traditional electrothermal desalination suffers from significant heat loss, which limits the improvement of the apparent energy efficiency, resulting in excessive energy consumption and a reliance on bulky equipment. Here we present an interlayer electrothermal evaporator (IEE) that reduces heat loss and energy consumption by nearly two-thirds compared with a bulk electrothermal evaporator. When the photothermal effect of solar energy is considered, the IEE attains an impressive apparent energy efficiency of 93.31% with a freshwater flux of 69.46 l m−2 h−1. Significantly, the IEE uses solar cells to supply green electricity and incorporates a Fresnel lens for solar energy concentration, constituting a portable freshwater production system for outdoor application. The device produces 1.64 l of freshwater within 8 h with an evaporator area of only 30.72 cm2, which is sufficient to meet the daily needs of individuals, even from challenging water sources such as sediment water, oily water, high-salinity wastewater and strongly acidic water. Therefore, this green energy-driven IEE system enables high-flux freshwater production across diverse scenarios, providing a sustainable and scalable solution to mitigate freshwater scarcity.

P508.user_provided_abstract: Electrocatalysis is central to electrified energy conversion technologies, including the production of fuels and chemicals from renewable electricity. In recent years, atomistic modeling based on density functional theory (DFT) has become an indispensable tool for catalysis researchers because it can provide a molecular-level perspective into catalytic reactivity that is otherwise inaccessible to experimental measurements. Computational electrocatalysis model inputs are intended to capture fundamental understanding of the complex interfacial environment of the catalytic active site, but rely on practical approximations that can affect the reliability of insights gained from DFT. This Perspective outlines a framework for rigorous and reproducible integration of theory and experiment in heterogeneous electrocatalysis research. We discuss state-of-the-art computational methods and sources of error in model development and interpretation. We describe opportunities for validation of theoretical models and experimental interpretations as it pertains to the structure of active sites, reaction energetics, and microkinetic modeling. We provide examples to help computational researchers develop models that move beyond obtaining qualitative agreement with reactivity trends, and toward the development of rigorous mechanistic insights that can be leveraged to predict promising new catalysts or operating conditions. Rigor and reproducibility are enhanced when theory and experiment have multiple nodes of connection, which enhances the longevity and robustness of conclusions and insights about electrocatalytic reactivity.
